sql-to-json.assumptionNote: Assumes standard INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (...), (...); syntax. The column list is read from the first statement and applied to every row.
benefits: Move data from SQL dumps into spreadsheets, APIs, or JavaScript without a database.
Faster than writing a throwaway script every time you need a quick conversion.
Handles the fiddly bits — NULLs, escaped quotes, commas inside strings — correctly.
Works offline and keeps sensitive data on your machine instead of a server.

faqs.a: Standard INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (row), (row); statements, including several INSERT statements pasted together. The column list is read from the first statement and applied to all rows.
NULL becomes null in JSON and an empty cell in CSV. The string 'NULL' inside quotes is kept as text — only the bare keyword NULL is treated as missing data.
They are handled correctly. In CSV output the field is wrapped in double quotes ("Ravi, Kumar") so spreadsheet apps read it as one cell.
faqs.q: What about commas inside text, like 'Ravi, Kumar'?

faqs.a: Yes, for the INSERT portion. Paste just the INSERT statements — CREATE TABLE lines and other dump metadata are ignored. Very large dumps should be split into smaller chunks first.
faqs.q: Does it work with MySQL dumps?

faqs.a: Not directly. Run the SELECT in your database tool, export or copy the result as INSERT statements, then paste those here. Many tools (phpMyAdmin, DBeaver) can export results as INSERTs.
faqs.q: Can I convert a SELECT query?

faqs.a: No. All parsing happens in your browser with JavaScript. Nothing you paste ever leaves your device.
faqs.q: Is my data sent to a server?

sql-to-json.formula:
Row i, column j: output[i][column_j] = parsed_value(tuple_i[j]).
JSON: [ { col1: v1, col2: v2 }, ... ] — one object per tuple.
CSV: header row of column names, then one row per tuple; a cell is escaped as "..." if it contains a comma, quote, or newline.
howTo: Copy your INSERT INTO ... VALUES statements from your database tool or SQL dump.
Paste them into the text box (or load the sample to see the expected format).
Choose JSON for an array of objects, or CSV for a spreadsheet-ready table.
Check the row and column counts, preview the output, then copy it or download the file.
keyFacts: Reads standard SQL: INSERT INTO table (col1, col2) VALUES (v1, v2), (v3, v4); — including multiple INSERT statements.
NULL becomes JSON null and an empty CSV cell; numbers stay numbers; quoted text stays text.
SQL-escaped quotes (O''Brien) are unescaped to a single quote (O'Brien).
CSV output follows the standard rules: fields with commas, quotes, or newlines are wrapped in double quotes, and inner quotes are doubled.
The column list is read once from the first INSERT and applied to every row.
sql-to-json.keywords: sql to json, sql to csv, insert to json converter, result set to csv, sql data converter

labels.errorNoInsert: No INSERT INTO statements were found in the text.
labels.errorNoValues: No value rows were found after VALUES.
labels.noInput: Paste SQL INSERT statements to see the converted result here.

limitations: Only INSERT ... VALUES statements are parsed — SELECT queries, CREATE TABLE, and stored procedures are ignored.
Exotic dialect syntax or multi-line string tricks may not parse; keep SQL standard.
Very large dumps (tens of thousands of rows) can make the browser tab slow — split them first.
Type detection is simple: it distinguishes numbers, NULL, and text, not dates or booleans specifically.

sql-to-json.quickAnswer: Paste your INSERT INTO ... VALUES statements, pick JSON or CSV, and the tool parses the columns and rows into a clean array of objects or a proper CSV table. Three rows with id, name, city and balance become a JSON array of three objects or a CSV with a header row. NULL becomes null (or an empty cell), numbers stay numbers, and quoted commas like 'Ravi, Kumar' are handled correctly.
sql-to-json.tagline: Turn SQL INSERT statements into JSON.
sql-to-json.workedExample:
SQL:
INSERT INTO customers (id, name, city, balance) VALUES
(1, 'Asha Verma', 'Jaipur', 1500.50),
(2, 'Ravi, Kumar', NULL, 230),
(3, 'O''Brien', 'Kochi', 0);

JSON:
[
  {"id": 1, "name": "Asha Verma", "city": "Jaipur", "balance": 1500.5},
  {"id": 2, "name": "Ravi, Kumar", "city": null, "balance": 230},
  {"id": 3, "name": "O'Brien", "city": "Kochi", "balance": 0}
]

CSV:
id,name,city,balance
1,Asha Verma,Jaipur,1500.5
2,"Ravi, Kumar",,230
3,O'Brien,Kochi,0

Note how NULL became an empty cell and the comma inside 'Ravi, Kumar' forced quotes.
